items.statement:
Assume full AC. Let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth embedded surface with nonempty boundary and a supplied finite smooth disk-and-band presentation, allowing nonorientability. Let an embedded product cylinder $W=[-1,1]\times D^2$ meet $F$ exactly in its two end disks, lying in the interior of $F$. Replace those disks by the lateral annulus $[-1,1]\times\partial D^2$ and round the two seams, leaving the rest fixed, to obtain $F'$. The normal-transfer pairing of $F'$ has the same signature as that of $F$.

More precisely, old homology basis curves can be chosen away from the two disks and extended by two classes $b,c$ to a basis for $H_1(F';\mathbb Z)$ in which the new pairing matrix is
$$\begin{pmatrix}G&v&0\\v^T&k&\delta\\0&\delta&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad k\in\mathbb Z,\quad\delta\in\{1,-1\},$$
where $G$ is the old matrix. The boundary link and its entire surface collar remain fixed. In particular, for common chosen boundary normal push-offs $K_i'$ of its components $K_i$, the quantity $e(F)=-\sum_i\operatorname{lk}(K_i,K_i')$ is unchanged, as is $\operatorname{sign}(B_F)+e(F)/2$.

citations.quote:
Assume full AC. Let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth embedded surface with nonempty boundary, possibly nonorientable, with a supplied finite smooth disk-and-band presentation. The ambient three-sphere has its standard orientation. For oriented integral multicurves $a,b\subset\operatorname{int}F$, let $\tau b$ be the cycle consisting of the two small normal pushes over $b$, oriented by projection to $b$. For a one-sided circle this is one circle mapping with degree two, rather than a choice of a single normal direction. Then
$B_F([a],[b])=\operatorname{lk}(a,\tau b)$ defines a well-defined symmetric integral bilinear pairing on $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, independently of representatives and sufficiently small normal pushes. Every integral homology class has an oriented multicurve representative, permitting integer coefficients. The pairing extends to rational homology, with quadratic form $q_F(x)=B_F(x,x)$ satisfying the normal-transfer linking identity.

For an embedded compact subsurface $A\subset F$ with such a finite presentation, the pairing on $A$ is the pullback of $B_F$ under inclusion. If $F$ is oriented and its boundary is one knot, its pairing has matrix $V+V^T$ in any integral basis, where $V$ is the positive-push Seifert matrix. Orientation-preserving ambient isotopies transport the pairing.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be an
oriented link with $r\ge1$ components and complement $X_L$,
([[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]), and let
$$\varphi:H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow\mathbb Z$$
be the **total linking homomorphism**, defined as the composite
$$H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow[\ \sim\ ]{\mathrm{Alex}}\widetilde H^1(L;\mathbb Z)\cong\bigoplus_{i=1}^rH^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow{\text{sum}}\mathbb Z,$$
where the first arrow is Alexander duality
([[thm-alexander-duality-for-compact-locally-contractible-subsets-of-a-sphere]]),
each $H^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ is the orientation-induced
identification, and the last map sums the $r$ coordinates. By
[[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]] the map $\varphi$
may again be written $\pi_1(X_L)\to H_1(X_L)\xrightarrow{\varphi}\mathbb Z$; we
denote both composites by $\varphi$ and set $K:=\ker\varphi$.

The **one-variable Alexander module** of $L$ is
$$A_L:=H_1(\widetilde{X_L};\mathbb Z),$$
the first singular homology of the connected infinite cyclic cover
$p:\widetilde{X_L}\to X_L$ classified by $K$
([[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]],
[[lem-subgroup-quotient-of-universal-cover]],
[[def-covering-map-and-evenly-covered-neighbourhoods]]), equipped with its
structure of module over $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$
([[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]) in which $t$ acts by the deck
transformation corresponding to the positive generator of
$\operatorname{Deck}(\widetilde{X_L}/X_L)\cong\mathbb Z$.

**Caveats.** The cover is the one classified by $K=\ker\varphi$; since $K$ is
normal the cover is regular and its deck group is
$\pi_1(X_L)/K\cong\mathbb Z$
([[def-regular-covering]], [[thm-regular-covering-characterizations]], [[cor-deck-group-of-a-regular-covering]],
[[def-deck-transformation-and-deck-group]]). The module $A_L$ is ordinary
integral homology of the cover, with the deck action as its module structure;
no twisting by a representation of the link group is used. The total linking
homomorphism satisfies $\varphi(\mu_i)=1$ for a meridian $\mu_i$ of any one
component, so $r\ge1$ is needed for $\varphi$ to be interesting and $A_L$
depends on the orientations of all components through this map.

For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, the sequence
$$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;G)\to H_n(U;G)\oplus H_n(V;G)\to H_n(X;G)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{n-1}(U\cap V;G)\to\cdots$$
is exact, with middle map $(u,v)\mapsto u+v$.

derivations.claim: Write $F_0$ for $F$ with the interiors of the two end disks removed. It is connected: paths can be detoured around either deleted disk in its annular collar. The disk-and-band charts retract $F$ onto a finite core graph, by the band-fiber and disk-star contractions used in [F1], so $H_2(F;\mathbb Z)=0$. Cover $F$ by slightly enlarged copies of $F_0$ and the disjoint union of its two removed disks. The overlap is two annuli. In [F3] the two overlap circles give $H_1=\mathbb Z^2$, the two disks have $H_1=0$, and the map from the overlap $H_0=\mathbb Z^2$ to the sum of the covering sets' degree-zero groups is injective, because its two components map to the two distinct disk components. Exactness therefore gives $0\to\mathbb Z^2\to H_1(F_0;\mathbb Z)\to H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\to0$, with the first map represented by the two new boundary circles $c_0,c_1$. Since the last group is free by [F1], choose an integral basis and cycle representatives in $F_0$, splitting this sequence. This verifies both the independence of the two new circles and the integral lifting of the old basis.

Cover the tube replacement by slightly enlarged copies of $F_0$ and its lateral annulus. Their overlap consists of two annuli near its ends. In [F3] its first homology maps into $H_1(F_0)\oplus H_1(\text{annulus})$ by identifying the two classes $c_0,c_1$ with the annular core, with the signs determined by their chosen directions. The kernel of the next degree-zero map is $\mathbb Z$, because both covering sets are connected and their overlap has two components. Hence the quotient of the first-homology sum contributes the old basis and one core class $c$, and one further class $b$ maps to a generator of that degree-zero kernel. It can be represented by a longitudinal arc on the tube, closed by an arc in connected $F_0$. The coefficients are all units in the core identifications, so this yields an integral basis consisting of the old classes, $b$ and $c$, with no torsion or index ambiguity. Seams and these arcs lie in finitely many smooth charts, so rounding supplies the corresponding finite smooth disk-and-band presentation of $F'$.

Take $c=\{0\}\times\partial D^2$ and let $D_c=\{0\}\times D^2$ be its meridian disk in $W$. Choose the old representatives and their sufficiently short normal pushes away from $W$; this is possible because their curves lie in the compact unchanged portion of $F_0$ away from its end circles. The linking of $c$ with each such transfer is zero: the disk $D_c$ misses them. In complement homology this follows directly from [F2], by removing small disks around any transverse intersections of a spanning disk and reading their boundaries as signed meridians; here there are none. The two normal pushes of $c$ are concentric circles in the same disk plane, displaced to radii slightly below and above one, so each has linking zero with $c$. Thus $B_{F'}(c,c)=0$, and its pairings with the old basis vanish. All old-old pairings equal those in $F$, since their normal pushes can be chosen identically in the unchanged surface.

Choose the longitudinal representative of $b$ to run along a constant angular direction near the middle of the tube and close outside $W$. Along that middle portion the surface normal is radial. Of the two transferred pushes of $b$, exactly the inward one meets $D_c$, once, and the outward one misses it. This remains true if $b$ is one-sided on the whole surface: its normal cover may be one connected circle, but over this middle segment it still has exactly those two sheets, with both directions induced from $b$. Its remaining transfer lies away from $D_c$. Removing a small disk about this single transverse intersection gives the meridian relation of [F2], so $B_{F'}(c,b)=\delta\in\{1,-1\}$. Symmetry in [F1] gives the reverse entry. Write $k=B_{F'}(b,b)$ and let $v$ be its pairings with the old basis. Together with step 3.1 this is exactly the displayed matrix.

Its last two-by-two block $D=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}k&\delta\\\delta&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ has determinant $-1$, hence one positive and one negative eigenvalue. Its inverse has top-left entry zero. The invertible block change of coordinates eliminating the mixed column $(v,0)$ has Schur complement $G-(v,0)D^{-1}(v,0)^T=G$. Consequently the enlarged form is congruent over $\mathbb Q$ to $G\oplus D$, and congruence preserves the dimensions of maximal positive and negative subspaces. The block $D$ contributes signature zero, proving signature preservation. The move was supported away from the original boundary and its collar. Thus identical chosen boundary normal push-offs compute both Euler quantities, so these are equal term by term. Their halves added to the equal signatures are equal as well.

boundaries.reason: A connected surface with nonempty boundary and an actual specified local modification are supplied.

boundaries.evidence: Step 5.1 allows an empty old matrix and obtains a signature-zero rank-two block.
Steps 3.1–4.1 compute one meridian disk and one longitudinal class.

boundaries.reason: An embedded product cylinder with two disjoint end disks is assumed.

boundaries.evidence: Step 5.1 fixes the original boundary link and its entire collar.
Step 5.1 retains full AC through the linking interfaces; basis and meridian selections are finite.

axioms.use: Full AC is inherited from the normal-transfer linking pairing and its linking-number interface; all surface homology and block-matrix calculations are finite.

risk_review.notes: Connected interior tube only, allowing a one-sided longitudinal class. Step2.1 proves an integral basis and step5.1 supplies the full Schur complement calculation; no disconnected-component tube case is asserted.

contract.proof_status_evidence: Literal current steps, actual complete original Gordon–Litherland article reading, and successful scoped checks. Independent owner review remains owed.

constructive_supplier_evidence.exact_read_body:
1.1 The supplied presentation retracts onto a finite graph: collapse each band along its interval fibers to its core and each disk to a finite radial star joining its band intervals. These contractions agree on attaching collars and can be performed in their finite disk and rectangle charts. An integral graph cycle has a finite collection of directed edge strands, with as many incoming as outgoing strands at every vertex. Realize the strands by parallel smooth arcs in the bands, with their directions transported through any band twist, and join the ends in each vertex disk. Finite smooth arcs in a disk can be drawn with finitely many transverse crossings, by using polygonal arcs and rounding their finitely many corners. Resolve each crossing by connecting incoming to outgoing arcs in a smaller disk. This changes the cycle by a boundary in that disk and leaves a finite disjoint union of oriented embedded circles with its original homology class. A small inward displacement keeps them in the interior. This proves the representative assertion without orienting $F$. [given, construct]

1.2 The round metric gives the normal line bundle of $F$. A sufficiently short closed normal interval bundle embeds in $S^3$: the normal exponential map has invertible differential along the zero section by [F3], a finite cover gives a common positive radius, and collisions at arbitrarily small radii would converge to a single base point and contradict a local inverse there. Boundary charts are first extended slightly across the boundary, so the same argument includes their interval fibers. The inverse is smooth by induction in the derivative formula in [F3]. Denote this embedded interval bundle by $N$, and its horizontal two-sheeted boundary cover by $\pi:\widetilde F\to F$. Its total space may be connected or disconnected. Round the corners along the vertical boundary away from any chosen multicurves, producing a smooth boundary surface $\Sigma=\partial N$ that retains their horizontal lifts. Both lifts of every oriented curve are oriented by projection. No global normal direction on $F$ has been selected. [given, F3, construct]

2.1 On singular chains in $F$ define $\tau\sigma$ to be the sum of the two lifts of a simplex $\sigma$ to $\widetilde F$. A simplex is contractible by its straight-line contraction to a vertex; it is path-connected and locally path-connected. Thus [F4] gives exactly one lift for each of the two points over that vertex. Restricting lifts to any face bijects the two lift sets, again by [F4]. Consequently $\partial\tau=\tau\partial$, and $\pi_\#\tau=2\operatorname{id}$. This construction works equally for the connected and disconnected cover and uses the sum of the entire lift set. Contracting normal fibers gives, for each cycle $a$, a finite singular two-chain in $N$ with boundary $\tau a-2a$, by triangulating the finitely many simplex prisms of that homotopy. [step 1.2, F4, construct, algebra]

3.1 Define $B_F([a],[b])=\operatorname{lk}(a,\tau b)$ using the representatives in step 1.1. If $a-a'=\partial C$ on $F$, then $C$ misses $\tau b$; hence the change in linking is zero by [F1] and the symmetry in [F2]. If $b-b'=\partial D$ on $F$, step 2.1 gives $\tau b-\tau b'=\partial(\tau D)$ off $F$, so this change also has linking zero with every component of $a$. Thus the value depends only on the two homology classes. Additivity of chain transfer and of linking gives integral bilinearity. Changing to another sufficiently small positive normal radius, or to different sufficiently small transverse normal representatives, is a homotopy in the complement of $F$ through normal fibers, so [F1] proves independence of the normal push. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, F1, F2, algebra]

4.1 To prove symmetry choose the representatives $a,b$ transverse on $F$, using finite perturbations of the disk-and-band arcs, and put $x=\tau a$, $y=\tau b\subset\Sigma$. Push a cycle on $\Sigma$ slightly outward or inward from $N$, writing superscripts $o,i$. The chain in step 2.1 misses $y^o$, since the latter is outside $N$. Therefore $2B_F([a],[b])=\operatorname{lk}(x,y^o)$; here pushing $y$ outward did not meet $a$. Shifting the disjoint pair $(x,y^o)$ together inward in the boundary collar gives $(x^i,y)$, so $2B_F([a],[b])=\operatorname{lk}(x^i,y)$. On the other hand $2B_F([b],[a])=\operatorname{lk}(y,x^o)=\operatorname{lk}(x^o,y)$ by [F2]. Thus their difference is $\operatorname{lk}(x^i,y)-\operatorname{lk}(x^o,y)$. Passing $x$ from the inward to the outward level crosses $y$ once for each transverse crossing of $x$ and $y$ on $\Sigma$. Its linking change is their signed surface intersection, with one fixed global sign. Indeed remove a small disk at each crossing from the traced annulus: its remaining boundary relation in the complement of $y$ expresses the change as the sum of these signed positive meridians, and [F1] evaluates each as one. Each point of $a\cap b$ has two lifts, one on each side of $F$. Their signs are opposite because the orientation of $\partial N$ induced by its outward normal reverses between the two horizontal sheets. Thus the total signed intersection of $x,y$ is zero. This proves $2B_F([a],[b])=2B_F([b],[a])$, and integral cancellation proves symmetry. [step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, F1, F2, construct, algebra]

5.1 If $F$ is oriented with one boundary knot, its transfer is the sum of positive and negative normal pushes. On a multicurve $a$, translating the disjoint pair $(a^-,a)$ together through the oriented normal collar gives $(a,a^+)$; symmetry in [F2] therefore identifies both self-linking terms. Hence $B_F([a],[a])=2\operatorname{lk}(a^+,a)$. By [F2] the right side is the quadratic form with matrix $V+V^T$. Every class has such a representative, and polarization of the symmetric bilinear forms in step 4.1 gives equality of the full pairings, not just of their diagonal values. This proves the stated matrix identification. [step 1.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, F2, algebra]

6.1 For a subsurface $A$, its normal line over each interior multicurve is the same as the normal line of $F$. The two transfer cycles and their linking values can therefore be chosen literally equal, proving pullback under inclusion, whether or not the inclusion on homology is injective. An orientation-preserving ambient isotopy transports the cycles and normal push homotopies and preserves their positive-meridian linking coefficients, so it transports $B_F$. Finally the finite graph in step 1.1 makes integral first homology free of finite rank; tensoring and clearing denominators extends the pairing uniquely to rational homology. Its diagonal satisfies the normal-transfer identity by step 3.1. All selections were finite within the supplied presentation, with full AC retained through the stated linking interfaces. [step 1.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, F1, F2, algebra] ∎
constructive_supplier_evidence.use: The finite disk-and-band core-graph contraction in proof1.1 is used to see H2(F)=0 before applying actual Mayer–Vietoris.

items.statement:
Assume full AC. In oriented $\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$, fix $R>2r>0$ and $\epsilon\in\{1,-1\}$. Let $M_\epsilon$ be the embedded Möbius band parametrized by
$$m(\theta,t)=((R+t\cos(\theta/2))\cos\theta,(R+t\cos(\theta/2))\sin\theta,-\epsilon t\sin(\theta/2)),\qquad |t|\le r,$$
with $(0,t)$ identified with $(2\pi,-t)$. Its core is oriented by increasing $\theta$. Its boundary is an unknot, its integral normal-transfer pairing is $[\epsilon]$ on the core generator, and its boundary normal framing has self-linking $2\epsilon$.

Let $F$ be any connected compact smooth embedded surface with nonempty boundary and a supplied finite smooth disk-and-band presentation. Form $F'$ as the separated boundary connected sum of $F$ with a small copy of $M_\epsilon$: the two surfaces lie in disjoint ball interiors, joined along chosen boundary arcs by an untwisted product band whose interior misses them, and whose normal collar is the product of the chosen boundary normal collars. Smooth the seams. Then the boundary link of $F'$ is ambient isotopic to that of $F$, its normal pairing is integrally congruent to $B_F\oplus[\epsilon]$, and its boundary normal Euler quantity satisfies $e(F')=e(F)-2\epsilon$, where $e(S)=-\sum_i\operatorname{lk}(K_i,K_i')$ for componentwise normal push-offs determined by its surface collar. Consequently
$$\operatorname{sign}(B_{F'})+\tfrac12e(F')=\operatorname{sign}(B_F)+\tfrac12e(F).$$
Neither surface is required to be orientable, and the boundary link may have any positive number of components.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented embedded circle in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ be the ordered integral basis and positive normal push-off convention used to define the Seifert matrix $V$ above. Every class of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ has a representative that is a finite integral sum of pairwise disjoint smooth oriented embedded circles in $F$. For such representatives $x$ and $y$, the sum of the pairwise linking numbers between the positive push-off of $x$ and $y$ depends only on $[x]$ and $[y]$, is independent of the sufficiently small positive push-off, and equals the bilinear extension of $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. The linking number of two disjoint oriented circle components is symmetric. In particular, the Seifert pairing is a well-defined bilinear map $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\times H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Z$.

For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, the sequence
$$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;G)\to H_n(U;G)\oplus H_n(V;G)\to H_n(X;G)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{n-1}(U\cap V;G)\to\cdots$$
is exact, with middle map $(u,v)\mapsto u+v$.

Let $D,D'$ be regular oriented diagrams of links $L,L'$. If the diagrams
differ by one oriented Reidemeister move or a planar isotopy, the links are
equivalent. The local Reidemeister replacement has a realization supported
in a ball over its move disk, after choosing lifts that agree outside that
ball. Comparing arbitrary realizing links may additionally require changing
their heights away from the move disk.

derivations.claim: The displayed map is well-defined and smooth across the identification because both normal coefficients change sign when $\theta$ increases by $2\pi$. Its projection to the round core circle has fibers the indicated straight normal intervals; $R>2r$ makes these intervals disjoint for different base points. Its derivative has the nonzero angular core component and the independent unit interval direction, so it is an embedding of the Möbius band. Along the core its interval tangent makes one half-turn, and the normal line to the band is its perpendicular line in the core's normal plane, also making that half-turn. Thus the normal transfer of the core has the same meridional winding as the boundary $K=\partial M_\epsilon$. On the coordinate normal disk with coordinates radial-outward and vertical, its winding is $-\epsilon$, as the boundary is traversed for $0\le\theta\le4\pi$. This disk orientation is opposite the positive meridian orientation: at $\theta=0$ the ordered triple of increasing angular tangent, radial-outward direction and vertical direction has determinant $-1$ in the ambient orientation. Hence its positive meridional winding is $\epsilon$. The zero-framed longitude has linking zero with the round core, so [F2] gives $B_{M_\epsilon}(c,c)=\epsilon$. Since the band retracts to its core, this proves its pairing matrix $[\epsilon]$.

Parametrize $K$ by the same formula with $t=r$ and $0\le\theta\le4\pi$. Its projection to the horizontal plane is regular and has just one double point: equal projected points must have angular parameters differing by $2\pi$, and their radii are equal precisely when $\cos(\theta/2)=0$, giving the pair $\theta=\pi,3\pi$. At that pair the radial derivatives are opposite nonzero numbers and the angular derivatives are nonzero, so the crossing is transverse; the heights are $-\epsilon r$ and $+\epsilon r$. The inner lobe is the interval $\pi\le\theta\le3\pi$, whose radius is at most $R$; the complementary outer lobe has radius at least $R$. Thus the interior of the inner lobe contains no other projected strand. A planar isotopy puts that inner lobe into a Reidemeister-I move disk, and [F4] removes the unique crossing. Choose the local smoothing of the remaining outer lobe to be a positive radial graph about the origin; away from the smoothing it is the graph $R+r\cos(\theta/2)$ for $-\pi\le\theta\le\pi$. Radial interpolation, extended over a surrounding polar annulus, carries this simple graph to a round circle. By [F4] the resulting diagram is an unknot. Thus $K$ is an unknot.

Let $T$ be the boundary of the radius-$r$ normal tube of the round core. The boundary $K$ lies on $T$ and has slope $2\lambda+\epsilon\mu$, where $\lambda$ is the zero-framed core longitude and $\mu$ the positive meridian fixed in step 1.1. Along $K$, the interval tangent of $M_\epsilon$ is the radial normal to $T$; its other tangent is tangent to $K$. Consequently its surface normal is tangent to $T$ and transverse to $K$. A short normal push of $K$ is homotopic in the complement of $K$ to its parallel push on $T$, and then radially outward to a parallel curve on a slightly larger tube. On that larger torus its class is still $2\lambda_o+\epsilon\mu_o$. The curve $\lambda_o$ chosen at the outermost radial point of the tube has linking zero with $K$: its horizontal spanning disk meets $K$ at its two zero-height points with opposite signs. The positive meridian disk bounded by $\mu_o$ meets $K$ twice with the same positive sign, giving linking two. These intersection counts are equivalently the positive-meridian homology computation of [F2], obtained by deleting little disks around the transverse intersections of each spanning disk. Therefore bilinearity gives $\operatorname{lk}(K,K')=2\cdot0+\epsilon\cdot2=2\epsilon$, so $e(M_\epsilon)=-2\epsilon$. Reversing the chosen orientation of $K$ reverses both cycles in this self-linking and changes none of these values.

For the boundary sum cover $F'$ by enlarged copies of the two surfaces together with half of the product band on each; their overlap is a disk and both sets are connected. Its exact sequence in [F3] gives $H_1(F';\mathbb Z)\cong H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\oplus H_1(M_\epsilon;\mathbb Z)$, with the inclusion of the old basis and the new core realizing this direct sum. Their representative curves and normal pushes can be retained inside their separate balls, away from the attachment. Each cross-linking is zero: a cycle inside one ball bounds a singular two-chain there, obtained by coning in a ball chart, and that chain misses the other ball. By [F2] this gives zero linking. The unchanged old block and the new block of step 1.1 therefore give $B_{F'}\cong B_F\oplus[\epsilon]$. The finite band construction and seam rounding supply a finite smooth disk-and-band presentation for the new surface.

The boundary component at the attachment is the connected sum of its original component $J$ with $K$; every other boundary component is unchanged. Its framed self-linking is additive for the supplied product attachment. To see this in complement homology, cut the neck at its middle product disk and cap the cut ends by two parallel short arcs, one for the boundary cycle and one for its normal push. The two trace rectangles of this reconnection can be chosen disjoint from the other cycle, since the attachment and its normal collar are untwisted products. Thus the original boundary cycle is homologous to $J+K$ in the complement of its pushed cycle, and the pushed cycle is homologous to $J'+K'$ in the complement of $J\cup K$. Applying [F2] twice gives $\operatorname{lk}(J\mathbin{\#}K,(J\mathbin{\#}K)')=\operatorname{lk}(J,J')+\operatorname{lk}(K,K')$, since the two cross terms lie in disjoint balls and vanish. All other component self-linkings stay fixed. Step 2.1 consequently gives $e(F')=e(F)-2\epsilon$. The same local sum with an unknot does not change the boundary link type: its separated unknot summand is removed using its spanning disk, or using the Reidemeister-I isotopy of step 1.2 before flattening the remaining planar boundary-sum arc. The support can be kept in the attachment ball and a collar of that arc, away from every other component.

The added one-dimensional form in step 2.2 has signature $\epsilon$, so the signature increases by $\epsilon$. Step 3.1 makes half the Euler quantity decrease by $\epsilon$. Their sum is unchanged, proving the formula. The argument used only separate ball supports, the supplied product attachment and the explicit sign computation of the standard Möbius band, and so applies to arbitrary orientability of $F$ and arbitrary nonempty boundary links.
